questions.question_text: The delusion that a familiar person has been replaced by an imposter is referred to as
questions.explanation: Capgras syndrome is the belief that a familiar person has been replaced by an imposter[cite: 6]. Capgras syndrome is a member of the unspecified type of delusional disorders[cite: 6]. There are variants of Capgras syndrome such as the delusion that familiar persons can assume the guise of strangers (Frégoli’s phenomenon) and the very rare delusion that familiar persons can change themselves into other persons at will (intermetamorphosis)[cite: 6]. Patients with Cotard syndrome (also known as delire de négation or nihilistic delusional disorder) complain of having lost not only possessions, status, and strength, but also their heart, blood, and intestines[cite: 6]. Each delusional disorder of the unspecified type is not only rare but may be associated with schizophrenia, dementia, epilepsy, and other organic disorders[cite: 6]. Olfactory reference syndrome is a subcategory of delusional disorder, somatic type, in which the patient has delusions of foul body odors or halitosis[cite: 6]. It differs from other delusions of the somatic type in that it has an earlier age of onset (mean of 25 years), male predominance, unmarried, and absence of past psychiatric treatment[cite: 6]. Conjugal paranoia is a delusional disorder of infidelity in which the patient has delusions that a spouse is being unfaithful[cite: 6]. The eponym Othello syndrome has been used to describe morbid jealousy that can arise from multiple concerns[cite: 6]. The delusion usually affects men, often those with no prior psychiatric illness[cite: 6]. It may appear suddenly and serve to explain a host of present and past events involving the spouse’s behavior[cite: 6]. The condition is difficult to treat and may diminish only on separation, divorce, or death of the spouse[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is true about brief psychotic disorder?

options.text: Approximately 10 percent of patients diagnosed retain the diagnosis.
Fifty percent of the cases evolve into either schizophrenia or major mood disorder.
There are clear distinguishing features between brief psychotic disorder and acute-onset schizophrenia on initial presentation.
Poor prognosis is associated with emotional turmoil.

correct_answer.text: Fifty percent of the cases evolve into either schizophrenia or major mood disorder.

correct_answers.text: Fifty percent of the cases evolve into either schizophrenia or major mood disorder.

questions.explanation: The course of brief psychotic disorder is found in the diagnostic criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IV-TR)[cite: 6]. It is a psychotic episode that lasts more than 1 day but less than 1 month, with eventual return to premorbid level of functioning[cite: 6]. Approximately 50 percent patients diagnosed with brief psychotic disorder retain this diagnosis; the other 50 percent evolve into either schizophrenia or a major affective disorder[cite: 6]. There are no apparent distinguishing features among brief psychotic disorder, acute-onset schizophrenia, and mood disorders with psychotic features on initial presentation[cite: 6]. Several prognostic features have been proposed to characterize the illness, but they are inconsistent across studies[cite: 6]. The good prognostic features are similar to those found in schizophreniform disorder, including acute onset of psychotic symptoms, confusion or emotional turmoil at the height of the psychotic episode, good premorbid functioning, the presence of affective symptoms, and a short duration of symptoms[cite: 6]. There is a relative dearth of information on the recurrence of brief psychotic episodes, however, so the course and prognosis of this disorder have not been well characterized[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: The differential diagnosis of brief psychotic disorder includes

options.text: psychotic disorder due to a general medical condition

questions.explanation: Sharing rapid onset of symptoms, brief psychotic disorder must be differentiated from substance-induced psychotic disorders and psychotic disorders due to a general medical condition[cite: 6]. A thorough medical evaluation, including a physical examination, laboratory studies, and brain imaging, helps rule out many of those conditions[cite: 6]. With only cross-sectional information, brief psychotic disorder is difficult to differentiate from other types of functional psychosis[cite: 6]. The relationship between brief psychotic disorder and both schizophrenia and affective disorders remains uncertain[cite: 6]. The DSM-IV-TR has made the distinction between brief psychotic disorder and schizophreniform disorder clearer by now requiring a full month of psychotic symptoms for the latter[cite: 6]. If psychotic symptoms are present longer than 1 month, the diagnoses of schizophreniform disorder, schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, mood disorders with psychotic features, delusional disorder, and psychotic disorder not otherwise specified need to be entertained[cite: 6]. If psychotic symptoms of sudden onset are present for less than 1 month in response to an obvious stressor, the diagnosis of brief psychotic disorder is strongly suggested[cite: 6]. Other diagnoses to differentiate include factitious disorder, malingering, and severe personality disorders, with consequent transient psychosis possible[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: All of the following are associated with a good prognosis in a brief psychotic disorder except
questions.explanation: Good prognostic features for brief psychotic disorders include good premorbid adjustment, few premorbid schizoid traits, a severe precipitating stressor, the sudden onset of symptoms, affective symptoms, confusion and perplexity during psychosis, little affective blunting, a short duration of symptoms, and the absence of schizophrenic relatives[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Mrs. P is a 47-year-old, divorced, unemployed woman who lived alone and who experienced chronic psychotic symptoms despite treatment with olanzapine (Zyprexa) 20 mg per day and citalopram (Celexa) 20 mg per day. She believed that she was getting messages from God and the police department to go on a mission to fight against drugs. She also believed that an organized crime group was trying to stop her in this pursuit. The onset of her illness began at age 20 years, when she experienced the first of several depressive episodes. She also described periods when she felt more energetic; was more talkative; had a decreased need for sleep; and was more active, sometimes cleaning her house throughout the night. About 4 years after the onset of her symptoms, she began to hear “voices” that became stronger when she was depressed but were still present and disturbed her even when her mood was euthymic. The case of Mrs. P is a classic presentation of
questions.explanation: The case of Mrs. P demonstrates a “classic” presentation of schizoaffective disorder[cite: 6]. Schizoaffective disorder has features of both schizophrenia and mood disorders[cite: 6]. Patients are diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder if they fit into one of six categories: (1) patients with schizophrenia who have mood symptoms, (2) patients with mood disorder who have symptoms of schizophrenia even when euthymic, (3) patients with both mood disorder and schizophrenia, (4) patients with a third psychosis unrelated to schizophrenia and mood disorder, (5) patients whose disorder is on a continuum between schizophrenia and mood disorder, and (6) patients with some combination of the above[cite: 6]. In the case of Mrs. P, clear depressive and hypomanic episodes are present in combination with continuous psychotic illness[cite: 6]. Schizophreniform disorder is an acute psychotic disorder that has a rapid onset and lacks a long prodromal phase[cite: 6]. Symptoms must last at least 1 month but less than 6 months[cite: 6]. In the case of Mrs. P, symptoms presented for more than 6 months and include depressive and manic symptoms that are not indicated in the diagnostic criteria for schizophreniform disorder[cite: 6]. Delusional disorder is diagnosed when a person exhibits nonbizarre delusions for at least 1 month’s duration that cannot be attributed to other psychotic disorders[cite: 6]. The mood of patients with delusional disorders is consistent with the content of the delusions (i.e., a person with persecutory delusions is suspicious)[cite: 6]. Mrs. P experiences depressive and manic episodes that do not appear to coincide with the content of her delusions[cite: 6]. Brief psychotic disorder is a psychotic condition that involves the sudden onset of psychotic symptoms and lasts 1 day or more but less than 1 month[cite: 6]. It can also include the presence of marked stressors (i.e., war, torture, serious medical illness)[cite: 6]. Mrs. P’s symptoms present too long to qualify for this diagnosis[cite: 6]. Acute and transient psychotic disorders are defined as psychotic conditions with an onset within 2 weeks and full remission within 1 to 3 months[cite: 6]. It is also a nonaffective psychotic disorder; therefore, Mrs. P’s mood symptoms and the duration of the illness rule out acute and transient psychotic disorders[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: In schizoaffective disorder, all of the following variables indicate a poor prognosis except
questions.explanation: The course and the prognosis of schizoaffective disorder are variable[cite: 6]. As a group, patients with this disorder have a prognosis intermediate between patients with schizophrenia and patients with mood disorders[cite: 6]. Patients with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, typically have a better prognosis[cite: 6]. A poor prognosis is associated with the depressive type of schizoaffective disorder[cite: 6]. A poor prognosis is also associated with the following variables: no precipitating factor, a predominance of psychotic symptoms, early or insidious onset, a poor premorbid history, and a positive family history of schizophrenia[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Folie á deux is another name for
questions.explanation: Folie à deux is another name for shared psychotic disorder[cite: 6]. Other references for the disorder are shared paranoid disorder, induced psychotic disorder, folie imposée, and double insanity[cite: 6]. The disorder is characterized by the transfer of delusions from one person to another[cite: 6]. The key features of the disorder are the unquestioning acceptance of the other individual’s delusional beliefs and the temporal sequence of development of the disorder, with one of the individuals having an earlier onset[cite: 6]. Both persons are closely associated for a long time and typically live together in relative social isolation[cite: 6]. Shared psychotic disorder usually involves two individuals but may involve more than two individuals, including entire family units[cite: 6]. Persecutory delusional beliefs are most commonly seen in shared psychotic disorder, comprising about 70 percent of patients in one study; however, religious, grandiose, and somatic delusions may also be observed[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: True statements concerning the treatment of shared psychotic disorder include all of the following except

options.text: Recovery rates have been reported to be as low as 10 percent.
The submissive person commonly requires treatment with antipsychotic drugs.
Psychotherapy for nondelusional members of the patient’s family should be undertaken.
Separation of the submissive person from the dominant person is the primary intervention.
The submissive person and the dominant person usually move back together after treatment.

correct_answer.text: Psychotherapy for nondelusional members of the patient’s family should be undertaken.

correct_answers.text: Psychotherapy for nondelusional members of the patient’s family should be undertaken.

questions.explanation: Psychotherapy for nondelusional members of the patient’s family is usually not necessary[cite: 6]. Clinical reports vary, but the prognosis is guarded—recovery rates have been reported to be as low as 10 percent[cite: 6]. The submissive person often requires treatment with antipsychotic drugs, as does the dominant person[cite: 6]. Separation of the submissive person from the dominant person is the primary intervention[cite: 6]. The submissive person and the dominant person usually move back together after treatment[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: The best-documented risk factor for delusional disorder is
questions.explanation: The cause of delusional disorder is unknown[cite: 6]. The epidemiological and clinical literature suggests that certain risk factors may be relevant to the etiology and deserve further research elaboration[cite: 6]. These risk factors are found in Table 14.1[cite: 6]. Whether they are risk predictors or simply characteristics or markers of the disorder is unknown[cite: 6]. Familial psychiatric disorder, including delusional disorder, is the best documented risk factor at present[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Delusional disorder may include
questions.explanation: Generally, in delusional disorders, the patient’s delusions are well systematized and have been developed logically[cite: 6]. The person may experience auditory or visual hallucinations, but these are not prominent features[cite: 6]. Tactile or olfactory hallucinations may be present and prominent if they are related to the delusional content or theme[cite: 6]. Examples are the sensation of being infested by bugs or parasites, associated with delusions of infestation, and the belief that one’s body odor is foul, associated with somatic delusions[cite: 6]. The person’s behavioral and emotional responses to the delusion appear to be appropriate[cite: 6]. Impairment of functioning is not marked and personality deterioration is minimal, if it occurs at all[cite: 6]. General behavior is neither obviously odd nor bizarre[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Delusional disorder

options.text: is more common in men than in women
is an early stage of schizophrenia
is caused by frontal lobe lesions

questions.explanation: Delusional disorder is less common than schizophrenia[cite: 6]. Its prevalence in the United States is estimated to be 0.03 percent—in contrast with 1 percent for schizophrenia and 5 percent for mood disorders[cite: 6]. The neuropsychiatric approach to delusional disorder derives from the observation that delusions are a common symptom in many neurological conditions, particularly those involving the limbic system and the basal ganglia[cite: 6]. No evidence indicates that the disorder is caused by frontal lobe lesions[cite: 6]. Long-term follow-up of patients with delusional disorder has found that their diagnoses are rarely revised as schizophrenia or mood disorders; hence, delusional disorder is not an early stage of schizophrenia or mood disorders[cite: 6]. Moreover, delusional disorder has a later onset than does schizophrenia or mood disorders[cite: 6]. The mean age of onset is 40 years; the disorder does not usually begin by age 20 years[cite: 6]. The disorder is slightly more common in women than in men[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Mr. T was 42 years old when he was brought to a psychiatrist for evaluation. He lived with his parents and four brothers. His chief complaint was that his business partner was trying to force him to quit by giving him too much work. Although he appeared outwardly calm, Mr. T complained of nervousness and restlessness. He also noted an inability to sleep at night, believing that his neighbor was making noise on purpose. Mr. T’s brother corroborated that the neighbor was being quite noisy at night and did not seem to respond to requests to be quieter. The psychiatrist prescribed hypnotic and anxiolytic medication. Three days later, the psychiatrist received a phone call from the patient’s brother, who requested that Mr. T be seen emergently. Upon arriving at the psychiatrist’s office, Mr. T appeared quite anxious and perplexed. He stated that the noises had grown louder and were now present throughout the day. He was also convinced that other people besides his neighbor and his business partner were trying to harm him. Mr. T’s brother now reported that Mr. T’s beliefs had no basis in reality. This case illustrates which of the following difficulties in diagnosing delusional disorder?

options.text: The initial report appears believable but is actually a delusion.
The initial report appears delusional but is actually true.
The patient believes the physician is in on the plot against him.
The patient is unwilling to provide information.

correct_answer.text: The initial report appears believable but is actually a delusion.

correct_answers.text: The initial report appears believable but is actually a delusion.

questions.explanation: The initial report in this case appears believable but is actually a delusion[cite: 6]. Upon the first evaluation, Mr. T’s complaint about noise seemed believable and was verified by his brother, but by the second visit 3 days later, it was clear that Mr. T’s complaints were delusions[cite: 6]. Delusions are false fixed beliefs not in keeping with the culture[cite: 6]. The diagnosis of delusional disorder is made when a person exhibits nonbizarre delusions of at least 1 month’s duration that cannot be attributed to other psychiatric disorders[cite: 6]. The first step in the clinical assessment is establishing whether a delusion exists[cite: 6]. Some statements that initially seem to be delusional may, in fact, be true[cite: 6]. In contrast, as in the above case, reports of circumstances that initially seem believable may be clearly identified as delusions as the symptoms worsen, the delusion becomes less encapsulated, or more information comes to light[cite: 6]. Certain behavioral features such as hypersensitivity, guardedness, evasiveness, secretiveness, litigiousness, overly detailed descriptions, hostility, and humorlessness are characteristic of delusional patients yet are not pathognomonic[cite: 6]. The patient may also be secretive and vague and may not voluntarily provide the clinician with necessary details[cite: 6]. At other times, the patient may see no need to convey information, believing that the interviewer is part of the “conspiracy” and already knowledgeable about its specifics[cite: 6]. For example, the patient may view the interview as a staged game in which both parties know the hidden meanings behind the overt text[cite: 6]. As a result, certain phrases are commonly heard from individuals with persecutory ideas in the context of delusional disorder (e.g., “Don’t play games with me,” “You know what ‘they’ have been doing”)[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Evidence that suggests delusional disorder is a separate entity from schizophrenia or mood disorders includes
questions.explanation: An issue that is central to attributing causation is whether delusional disorder represents a separate group of conditions or is an atypical form of schizophrenic and mood disorders[cite: 6]. The relevant data come from a limited number of studies and are inconclusive[cite: 6]. Epidemiology data suggest that delusional disorder is a separate condition; it is far less prevalent than schizophrenic or mood disorders; the age of onset is later than in schizophrenia, although men tend to experience the illness at earlier ages than women; and the sex ratio is different from that of mood disorder, which occurs disproportionately among women[cite: 6]. Findings from family or genetic studies also support the theory that delusional disorder is a distinct entity[cite: 6]. If delusional disorder is simply an unusual form of schizophrenic or mood disorders, the incidence of these latter conditions in family studies of delusional disorder patient probands should be higher than that of the general population[cite: 6]. However, this has not been a consistent finding[cite: 6]. A recent study concluded that patients with delusional disorder are more likely to have family members who show suspiciousness, jealousy, secretiveness, even paranoid illness, than families of controls[cite: 6]. Other investigative efforts have found paranoid personality disorder and avoidant personality disorder to be more common in the relatives of patients with delusional disorder than in the relatives of control subjects or of schizophrenic patients[cite: 6]. A recent study documented modest evidence for an increased risk of alcoholism among the relatives of patients with delusional disorder compared with probands with schizophrenia, probands with psychotic disorder not otherwise specified, and probands with schizophreniform disorder[cite: 6]. Investigations into the patient’s natural history also lend support to the suggestion that delusional disorder is a distinct category: age of onset appears to be later than in schizophrenia, and outcome is generally better for delusional patients with disorder than for those with schizophrenia[cite: 6]. Although fraught with methodological shortcomings, premorbid personality data indicate that people with schizophrenia and those with delusional disorder differ early in life[cite: 6]. The former are more likely to be introverted, schizoid, and submissive and the latter extroverted, dominant, and hypersensitive[cite: 6]. Patients with delusional disorder may have below-average intelligence[cite: 6]. Precipitating factors, especially related to social isolation, conflicts of conscience, and immigration, are more closely associated to delusional disorder than schizophrenia[cite: 6]. These characteristics support the view that environmental factors may play an important etiological role[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: True statements about patients with delusional disorder, erotomanic type, include:

options.text: They exhibit what has been called “paradoxical conduct.”
The course of the disorder is invariably chronic.
Separation from the love object is usually not an effective treatment.

correct_answer.text: They exhibit what has been called “paradoxical conduct.”

correct_answers.text: They exhibit what has been called “paradoxical conduct.”

questions.explanation: Patients with erotomania have delusions of secret lovers[cite: 6]. Most frequently, the patient is a woman, but men are also susceptible to the delusion[cite: 6]. The patient believes that a suitor, usually more socially prominent than herself, is in love with her[cite: 6]. The onset can be sudden, and the delusion becomes the central focus of the patient’s existence[cite: 6]. Patients with erotomania frequently show certain characteristics: they are generally but not exclusively women; may be considered unattractive in appearance; are in low-level jobs; and lead withdrawn, lonely lives, being single and having few sexual contacts[cite: 6]. They select secret lovers who are substantially different from themselves[cite: 6]. They exhibit what has been called “paradoxical conduct,” the delusional phenomenon of interpreting all denials of love as secret affirmations of love[cite: 6]. The course may be chronic, recurrent, or brief[cite: 6]. Separation from the love object may be the only satisfactory means of intervention[cite: 6]. Although men are less commonly affected by this condition than women, they may be more aggressive and possibly violent in their pursuit of love[cite: 6]. Hence, in forensic populations, men with this condition predominate[cite: 6]. The object of aggression may not be the loved individual but companions or protectors of the love object, who are viewed as trying to come between the lovers[cite: 6]. The tendency toward violence among men with erotomania may lead initially to police rather than psychiatric contact[cite: 6]. In certain cases, resentment and rage in response to an absence of reaction from all forms of love communication may escalate to a point that the love object is in danger[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: The following statements about psychotherapeutic treatment of delusional disorders is true except

options.text: It is essential that the patient trust the therapist.
The therapist should not challenge the patient’s delusions.
Empathy toward the patient’s struggle with the delusion is useful.
Individual therapy seems to be less effective than group therapy.
When available, family members should be involved in therapy.

correct_answer.text: Individual therapy seems to be less effective than group therapy.

correct_answers.text: Individual therapy seems to be less effective than group therapy.

questions.explanation: The use of individual therapy in the treatment of patients with delusional disorders seems to be more (not less) effective than group therapy[cite: 6]. The essential element in effective psychotherapy is to establish a relationship in which the patient begins to trust the therapist[cite: 6]. Initially, the therapist should neither agree with nor challenge the patient’s delusions[cite: 6]. Although the therapist must ask about a delusion to establish its extent, persistent questioning about it should probably be avoided[cite: 6]. The physicians may stimulate the motivation to receive help by emphasizing a willingness to help the patient with his or her anxiety or irritability without suggesting that the delusions be treated, but the therapist should not actively support the notion that the delusions are real[cite: 6]. A useful approach in building a therapeutic alliance is to empathize with the patient’s internal experience of being overwhelmed by persecution[cite: 6]. It may be helpful to make such comments as, “You must be exhausted, considering what you have been through.”[cite: 6] Without agreeing with every delusional misperception, a therapist can acknowledge that from the patient’s perspective, such perceptions create much distress[cite: 6]. The ultimate goal is to help the patient entertain the possibility of doubt about his or her perceptions[cite: 6]. When family members are available, clinicians may decide to involve them in the treatment plan[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Of the following somatic treatments for delusional disorder, which is considered the least likely to be successful?

options.text: All of the above are considered equally effective

questions.explanation: Patients with delusional disorders respond less well generally to electroconvulsive treatment than do patients with major mood disorders with psychotic features[cite: 6]. Some patients may respond to selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRIs), especially cases of body dysmorphic disorder with delusional concerns[cite: 6]. Dopamine-receptor antagonists (DRAs) (particularly pimozide [Orap]), serotonin-dopamine antagonists (SDAs), and SSRIs are pharmacological agents with reports of successful use in delusional disorder[cite: 6]. Delusional disorder is a psychotic disorder by definition, and the natural presumption has been that patients with the condition would respond to antipsychotic medication[cite: 6]. Because controlled studies are limited and the disorder is uncommon, the results required to support this practice empirically have been only partially obtained[cite: 6]. The disparate findings in the recent literature on delusional disorder treatment have been summarized recently, with several qualifications[cite: 6]. Of approximately 1,000 articles published since 1961, the majority since 1980, 257 cases of delusional disorder (consistent with DSM-IV-TR criteria), of which 209 provided sufficient treatment detail to make comparison, were assessed[cite: 6]. Overall treatment results indicated that 80.8 percent of patients recovered either fully or partially[cite: 6]. Pimozide (the most frequently reported treatment) produced full recovery in 68.5 percent and partial recovery in 22.4 percent of patients treated, and there was full recovery in 22.6 percent and partial recovery in 45.3 percent of patients treated with DRAs that are typical neuroleptic agents (e.g., thioridazine [Mellaril], haloperidol [Haldol], chlorpromazine [Thorazine], loxapine [Loxitane], perphenazine [Trilafon], and others)[cite: 6]. The remaining patients were noncompliant with any treatment[cite: 6]. There were no specific conclusions drawn regarding treatment with SSRIs, although a number of such reports have been published[cite: 6]. The results of treatment with the SDAs (i.e., clozapine [Clozaril], risperidone [Risperdal], olanzapine [Zyprexa], and others) are preliminary[cite: 6]. Unfortunately, systematic case series will develop slowly, but these early results suggest that the atypical neuroleptic agents may add to the available treatment options[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: The postpartum blues

options.text: occurs in up to 50 percent of women after childbirth
begins shortly after childbirth and lessens in severity over the course of 1 week

questions.explanation: The so-called postpartum blues is a normal condition that occurs in up to 50 percent of women after childbirth[cite: 6]. Postpartum blues is self-limited; lasts only a few days; and is characterized by tearfulness, fatigue, anxiety, and irritability that begin shortly after childbirth and lessen in severity over the course of 1 week[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Postpartum psychosis

options.text: occurs more commonly in multigravida women
is rarely correlated with perinatal complications
almost always begins within 8 weeks of delivery
usually occurs abruptly, with no prodromal psychotic symptoms
is essentially an episode of a psychotic disorder

correct_answer.text: almost always begins within 8 weeks of delivery

correct_answers.text: almost always begins within 8 weeks of delivery

questions.explanation: The symptoms of postpartum psychosis most often begin within 8 weeks of delivery[cite: 6]. About 50 to 60 percent of affected women with postpartum psychosis have just had their first child, and in that group, half of the newborns have perinatal complications[cite: 6]. The onset of florid psychotic symptoms is usually preceded by prodromal signs, such as insomnia, restlessness, agitation, lability of mood, and mild cognitive deficits[cite: 6]. The most robust data indicate that postpartum psychosis is related to a mood disorder, usually a bipolar disorder[cite: 6]. Relatives of those with postpartum psychosis have an incidence of mood disorders that is similar to the incidence in relatives of persons with mood disorders[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: All of the following are true statements about postpartum psychosis except

options.text: Generally, it is not considered a psychiatric emergency.
Delusional material may involve the idea that the baby is dead.
The risk is increased if the patient had a recent mood disorder.
Hallucinations involve voices telling the patient to kill her baby.
It is found in one to two per 1,000 deliveries.

correct_answer.text: Generally, it is not considered a psychiatric emergency.

correct_answers.text: Generally, it is not considered a psychiatric emergency.

questions.explanation: Postpartum psychosis is found in one to two per 1,000 deliveries[cite: 6]. The risk is increased if the patient or the patient’s mother had a previous postpartum illness or mood disorder[cite: 6]. The symptoms are usually experienced within days of delivery and almost always within the first 8 weeks after giving birth[cite: 6]. The patient begins to complain of insomnia, restlessness, and fatigue, and she shows lability of mood with tearfulness[cite: 6]. Later symptoms include suspiciousness, confusion, incoherence, irrational statements, and obsessive concerns about the baby’s health[cite: 6]. Delusional material may involve the idea that the baby is dead or defective[cite: 6]. The birth may be denied, or ideas of persecution, influence, or perversity may be expressed[cite: 6]. Hallucinations may involve voices telling the patient to kill her baby[cite: 6]. Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency[cite: 6]. In one study, 5 percent of patients killed themselves, and 4 percent killed the baby[cite: 6]. Postpartum psychosis is not to be confused with postpartum “blues.”[cite: 6]

questions.question_text: Most studies of normal pregnant women indicate that the percentage who report the “blues” in the early postpartum period is about
questions.explanation: Postpartum psychosis should not be confused with postpartum “blues,” a normal condition that occurs in about 50 percent of women after childbirth[cite: 6]. The “blues” are self-limited; last only a few days; and are characterized by tearfulness, fatigue, anxiety, and irritability that begin shortly after childbirth and lessen in severity each day postpartum[cite: 6]. Postpartum psychosis is characterized by agitation, severe depression, and thoughts of infanticide[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Attaque de nervios

options.text: is usually associated with acute fear
usually results in a deteriorating course
is most common in Puerto Ricans
usually has no precipitating stressful event
usually features a sense of being out of control

correct_answer.text: usually features a sense of being out of control

correct_answers.text: usually features a sense of being out of control

questions.explanation: A general feature of attaque de nervios is a sense of being out of control[cite: 6]. Attaque de nervios is reported in Latinos from throughout the Caribbean and it is not most common among Puerto Ricans[cite: 6]. It also occurs in South America and Mediterranean countries[cite: 6]. It frequently occurs as a direct result of a stressful event relating to the family[cite: 6]. It most closely resembles a panic attack, but unlike panic attacks, it is associated with a precipitating event[cite: 6]. Panic attacks occur spontaneously[cite: 6]. Persons may experience amnesia for what occurred during the attack, but they otherwise return rapidly to their usual level of functioning[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Erotomania is also referred to as
questions.explanation: Erotomania, the delusional disorder in which the person makes repeated efforts to contact the object of the delusion through letters, phone calls, gifts, visits, surveillance, and even stalking, is also called Clérambault’s syndrome[cite: 6]. Most patients with erotomania are women[cite: 6]. In forensic samples in which harm is done to another person, most patients are men[cite: 6]. In Cotard’s syndrome, patients may believe that they have lost everything: possessions, strength, and even bodily organs[cite: 6]. Fregoli’s syndrome is the delusion that a persecutor is taking on a variety of faces, like an actor[cite: 6]. Ganser’s syndrome is the voluntary production of severe psychiatric symptoms, sometimes described as the giving of approximate answers (e.g., 2 + 2 = 5)[cite: 6]. Capgras syndrome is the delusion that familiar people have been replaced by identical impostors[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Puerperal psychosis

options.text: is most likely to occur in patients with a previous history of the disorder
usually does not occur until 2 to 3 months postpartum
has a prevalence of 10 to 15 percent

correct_answer.text: is most likely to occur in patients with a previous history of the disorder

correct_answers.text: is most likely to occur in patients with a previous history of the disorder

questions.explanation: Puerperal psychosis is the most severe form of postpartum psychiatric illness[cite: 6]. In contrast to postpartum blues and depression, puerperal psychosis is a rare event that occurs in approximately one to two per 1,000 women after childbirth[cite: 6]. Its presentation is often dramatic, with onset of psychosis as early as the first 48 to 72 hours postpartum[cite: 6]. Most women with puerperal psychosis develop symptoms within the first 2 to 4 weeks after delivery[cite: 6]. In women with this disorder, psychotic symptoms and disorganized behavior are prominent and cause significant dysfunction[cite: 6]. Puerperal psychosis resembles a rapidly evolving affective psychosis with restlessness, irritability, and insomnia[cite: 6]. Women with this disorder may exhibit a rapidly shifting depressed or elated mood, disorientation or depersonalization, and disorganized behavior[cite: 6]. Delusional beliefs often center on the infant and include delusions that the child may be defective or dying, that the infant has special powers, or that the child is either Satan or God[cite: 6]. Auditory hallucinations that instruct the mother to harm or kill herself or her infant are sometimes reported[cite: 6]. Although most believe that this illness is indistinguishable from an affective (or manic) psychosis, some have argued that puerperal psychosis may be clinically distinct in that it is more commonly associated with confusion and delirium than nonpuerperal psychotic mood disorder[cite: 6]. Although it has been difficult to identify specific demographic and psychosocial variables that consistently predict risk for postpartum illness, there is a well-defined association between all types of postpartum psychiatric illness and a personal history of mood disorder (Table 14.2)[cite: 6]. At highest risk are women with a history of postpartum psychosis; up to 70 percent of women who have had one episode of puerperal psychosis will experience another episode after a subsequent pregnancy[cite: 6]. Similarly, women with histories of postpartum depression are at significant risk, with rates of postpartum depression recurrence as high as 50 percent[cite: 6]. Women with bipolar disorders also appear to be particularly vulnerable during the postpartum period, with rates of bipolar relapse ranging from 20 to 50 percent[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Acute and transient psychotic disorder

options.text: can be definitively diagnosed without an extensive past history
is easily recognized early in its course
is often only definitively diagnosed retrospectively
may have a better outcome with acute onset
has a higher age of onset in developing countries

correct_answer.text: is often only definitively diagnosed retrospectively

correct_answers.text: is often only definitively diagnosed retrospectively

questions.explanation: A definitive diagnosis of acute and transient psychotic disorder is often only possible retrospectively and with (not without) extensive information on the patient’s past history[cite: 6]. Acute and transient psychotic disorders are defined by the tenth edition of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-10) as psychotic conditions with onset within 2 weeks and full remission within 1 to 3 months[cite: 6]. These conditions do not have a designated place in the DSM-IV-TR[cite: 6]. Many of the cases of ICD-10 acute and transient psychotic disorders would be categorized as schizophreniform disorder, brief psychotic disorder, or psychotic disorder not otherwise specified in the DSM-IV-TR[cite: 6]. The age of onset in developing countries appears to be lower (not higher) than in industrialized settings[cite: 6]. Recognition of acute and transient psychotic disorders early in their course is difficult (not easy)[cite: 6]. In the first few weeks of the illness, there are no specific indicators that would distinguish acute and transient disorder from other nonaffective psychotic disorders with acute onset[cite: 6]. Furthermore, even in retrospect, it is often difficult to assess the duration of a psychotic episode or distinguish spontaneous remission from remission caused by antipsychotic medication treatment[cite: 6]. The ICD-10 also suggests that a distinction be made between acute onset (i.e., onset within 2 weeks) and abrupt onset (i.e., onset within 48 hours), noting that the latter may be associated with even better outcome[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: A 13-year-old girl presents to clinic for unusual behavior. Her father states that for the past 3 months, his daughter claims she has been “communicating with unidentified flying objects from outer space.” During this period, it has become increasingly difficult to communicate with his daughter, and she has become an introvert. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Because symptoms are present for more than 1 month but less than 6 months, the diagnosis of schizophreniform disorder is likely[cite: 6]. The patient is presenting with hallucinations and negative symptoms[cite: 6]. In schizophreniform disorder, the diagnosis must include at least two of any of the following: disorganized speech or behavior, negative symptoms, delusions, and hallucinations[cite: 6]. Schizophrenia would present with symptoms for at least 6 months[cite: 6]. The diagnosis of brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms be present for at least 1 day but less than 1 month[cite: 6]. Diagnosis requires one or more of hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized behavior or speech[cite: 6]. Schizoaffective disorder may be diagnosed when a mood disorder and schizophrenia are both present[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Mood symptoms are present
questions.explanation: Schizoaffective disorder has features of both schizophrenia and mood disorders[cite: 6]. Patients must fit into one of six categories: (1) patients with schizophrenia who have mood symptoms, (2) patients with mood disorder who have symptoms of schizophrenia during periods of euthymia, (3) patients with both mood disorder and schizophrenia, (4) patients with a psychosis unrelated to schizophrenia as well as a mood disorder, (5) patients whose disorder is on a continuum between schizophrenia and mood disorder, and (6) patients with some combination of the above[cite: 6]. However, it can be difficult to diagnose[cite: 6]. The clinician must accurately diagnose the mood disorder, making sure it meets the criteria of either a manic or a depressive episode but also determining the exact length of each episode (not always easy or even possible)[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Return to baseline state within 6 months
questions.explanation: By definition, patients with schizophreniform disorder return to their baseline state within 6 months[cite: 6]. However, in some cases, the illness is episodic with more than one episode occurring after long periods of full remission[cite: 6]. Some studies show that 45 to 75 percent of schizophreniform patients may progress to schizophrenia with longitudinal assessment[cite: 6]. Schizophreniform disorder is an acute psychotic disorder that has a rapid onset and lacks a long prodromal phase[cite: 6]. The initial symptom profile is the same as schizophrenia in that two or more psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech and behavior, or negative symptoms) must be present[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: May progress to schizophrenia
questions.explanation: By definition, patients with schizophreniform disorder return to their baseline state within 6 months[cite: 6]. However, in some cases, the illness is episodic with more than one episode occurring after long periods of full remission[cite: 6]. Some studies show that 45 to 75 percent of schizophreniform patients may progress to schizophrenia with longitudinal assessment[cite: 6]. Schizophreniform disorder is an acute psychotic disorder that has a rapid onset and lacks a long prodromal phase[cite: 6]. The initial symptom profile is the same as schizophrenia in that two or more psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech and behavior, or negative symptoms) must be present[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Prominent hallucinations are absent
questions.explanation: Patients with delusional disorder, by definition, do not have prominent or sustained hallucinations[cite: 6]. The diagnosis of delusional disorder is made when a person exhibits nonbizarre delusions of at least 1 month’s duration that cannot be attributed to other psychotic disorders[cite: 6]. There are five subtypes of delusional disorders: (1) persecutory type (the belief by the patient that he or she is being persecuted or harmed), (2) jealous type (i.e., the belief that one’s spouse is unfaithful), (3) erotomanic type (the belief that another person, usually of higher status, is in love with the patient), (4) somatic type (delusions of a hypochondriacal or somatic nature), and (5) grandiose type (delusions of grandeur)[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: The presence of acute stress within 2 weeks of onset
questions.explanation: Acute and transient psychotic disorders are defined by the ICD-10 as psychotic conditions with onset within 2 weeks and full remission within 1 to 3 months[cite: 6]. The ICD-10 provides a sequence of three “key features” to be used for diagnosing acute and transient psychotic disorders[cite: 6]. In order of priority, these features are (1) an acute onset (within 2 weeks); (2) the presence of typical syndromes, which are the basis for the subcategorization into specific disorders; and (3) the presence of associated acute stress (within about 2 weeks of onset)[cite: 6]. Acute onset is defined as “a change from a state without psychotic features to a clearly abnormal psychotic state, within a period of 2 weeks or less.”[cite: 6]

questions.question_text: Psychomotor retardation
questions.explanation: Psychomotor retardation is a general slowing of mental and physical activity[cite: 6]. It is often a sign of a major depressive episode, which is characterized by feelings of sadness, loneliness, despair, low self-esteem, and self-reproach[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Thought broadcasting
questions.explanation: Thought broadcasting is the feeling that one’s thoughts are being broadcast or projected into the environment[cite: 6]. Such feelings are encountered in schizophrenia[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Easy distractibility with an elevated, expansive, or irritable mood
questions.explanation: A patient in a manic episode is easily distracted, with an elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with pressured speech and hyperactivity[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Nonbizarre persecutory or grandiose delusions
questions.explanation: Delusional disorder is characterized by nonbizarre persecutory or grandiose delusions and related disturbances in mood, thought, and behavior[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Suspiciousness and mistrust of people without psychotic symptoms
questions.explanation: The essential feature of paranoid personality disorder is a long-standing suspiciousness and mistrust of people without the presence of psychotic symptoms[cite: 6]. Patients with this disorder are hypersensitive and continually alert for environmental clues that will validate their original prejudicial ideas[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Cognitive disorders
questions.explanation: In cognitive disorders, such as dementia, delusions secondary to perceptual disturbances are most often evident[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Delusional disorder
questions.explanation: In delusional disorder, delusions of jealousy are most commonly found[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Depressive disorders
questions.explanation: In depressive disorders, delusions of guilt are especially characteristic[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Mania
questions.explanation: Grandiose delusions are most often seen in mania but can be observed in other psychotic disorder as well[cite: 6].

questions.question_text: Schizophrenia
questions.explanation: In schizophrenia, bizarre delusions may occur (e.g., of being controlled by outside persons or forces and delusions of persecution)[cite: 6].
